The quotient has one node per block, labeled block_0, block_1 and block_2; edges inside a block vanish and the several edges between two blocks merge into one." width="100%"} Each block (group of nodes) in the partition becomes a single node in the quotient graph. Edges between different blocks become edges in the quotient. Edges within the same block are removed. The quotient graph is a "zoomed-out" view of a network: it shows which groups are connected to which, without the detail inside each group. Typical uses: - turning a community detection result into a community-level network, to see which communities talk to each other - aggregating a network by a categorical attribute (e.g., departments, countries, or cell types) to study group-to-group connectivity - coarsening a large graph before layout or further analysis Two blocks are joined by a single edge whenever at least one original edge runs between them; the number of such edges is not recorded, and the quotient edge takes the weight and attributes of the first original edge found. Directed graphs give a directed quotient, so `A -> B` and `B -> A` between blocks produce two quotient edges. Unlike `contract_nodes_multi()`, which collapses one group and keeps the rest of the graph, this method collapses every block at once and replaces node identities entirely. The original graph is not modified. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [partition]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[list[int | str]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of node groups. Each inner list contains node IDs or labels belonging to the same block. Every node must appear exactly once. The order of the blocks determines the quotient node IDs and labels: block `i` (0-based) becomes the node with ID `i + 1` and label `"block_i"`. An empty inner list produces an isolated quotient node. A common way to build this list is to group the output of a community detection method by community ID. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new quotient graph where each partition block is a node. Nodes are labeled `"block_0"`, `"block_1"`, etc., in partition order. Since a block replaces several original nodes, it doesn't inherit their attributes; instead its `members` attribute lists the original node IDs it contains, in ascending order. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [KeyError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If any node ID in the partition does not exist. [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If a label in the partition is not found, if a node appears in multiple blocks, or if some nodes are missing. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} A quotient graph is what you get when you glue an equivalence relation onto a graph: each block of the partition collapses to a single new node, and any edge crossing between blocks becomes an edge in the quotient. Intra-block edges are discarded, so the quotient never carries self-loops regardless of how they arose. Every original node must appear in exactly one block; a validation pass raises `ValueError` otherwise. Weights come from the first inter-block edge encountered per pair (they are not summed), which is fine when weights encode capacity but worth reviewing when they encode length or cost. Nodes in the returned graph are relabeled `block_0`, `block_1`, and so on, matching partition order. Quotients power community-level analysis, hierarchical coarsening, and the algebraic view of graph homomorphisms. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Splitting a six-node path into two halves gives a quotient with two nodes, joined by a single edge that comes from the original edge `3-4`: ::: {#d2bb7a2e .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(directed=False) g.add_path_graph(6) # 1 -- 2 -- 3 -- 4 -- 5 -- 6 # Partition: {1,2,3} and {4,5,6} partition = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]] quotient = g.quotient_graph(partition) quotient.count_nodes(), quotient.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (2, 1) ``` ::: ::: Labels work too. Here three groups are joined by several original edges, but each pair of groups gets only one quotient edge, labelled by block: ::: {#64e9bc6f .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph(directed=False) g.add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]) g.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), ("C", "D"), ("B", "D"), ("D", "E"), ("E", "F"), ("C", "F")]) quotient = g.quotient_graph([["A", "B", "C"], ["D", "E"], ["F"]]) quotient.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['block_0--block_1', 'block_1--block_2', 'block_0--block_2'] ``` ::: ::: A typical workflow builds the partition from community detection. Grouping the `cmty_louvain()` output by community ID yields one block per community, and the quotient shows how the communities connect: ::: {#fda1f6dc .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} from collections import defaultdict g = ec.Graph(directed=False) g.add_path_graph(20) membership = g.cmty_louvain(return_dict=True) communities = defaultdict(list) for node, comm in membership.items(): communities[comm].append(node) partition = list(communities.values()) quotient = g.quotient_graph(partition) # Number of communities and of community-to-community links quotient.count_nodes(), quotient.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (5, 4) ``` ::: :::
